articles.title: House Dems overwhelmingly reject anti-socialism resolution after 2 moderates defy Jeffries
articles.summary: House Democrats were split on a vote to condemn socialism after two Democrats helped Republicans push their agenda forward.
articles.body: The House of Representatives passed a resolution condemning socialism on Tuesday evening, with all but eight House Democrats voting against it. The resolution passed 220 to 192 with all "no" votes coming from the left, including Democrats’ senior leaders: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., House Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif. The legislation also affirmed support for election integrity and called for passage of the Safeguarding American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, which nearly all Democrats oppose. In a stunning twist of fate, however, the vote would not have occurred if two House Democrats hadn't stepped in hours earlier to help the GOP through a procedural hurdle — blindsiding Jeffries in the process. JOHNSON SCORES WIN AS CONSERVATIVE REBELS END HOUSE FLOOR BLOCKADE OVER VOTER ID BILL House conservatives had threatened to tank a procedural vote, called a "rule vote," meant to unlock debate on several bills GOP leaders wanted lawmakers to vote on this week. That included the resolution condemning socialism and several other unrelated bills. Five Republicans voted against the rule, which was poised to fail until Reps. Jared Golden, D-Maine, and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., provided two critical votes to get the GOP over the finish line in a narrow 209 to 208 vote. All Republicans wound up voting in favor of the resolution condemning socialism and affirming election integrity on Tuesday evening, however. TENSIONS ERUPT IN HOUSE HEARING AS GOP ADVANCES ANTI-SOCIALISM RESOLUTION WHILE DEMS RAGE: 'SILLY SEASON' Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez were among the Democrats who joined the GOP in that vote, as well as Reps. Don Davis, D-N.C., Vicente Gonzalez, D-Texas, Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, Kathy Castor, D-Fla., Gabe Vasquez, D-N.M., and Darren Soto, D-Fla. Reps. Maggie Goodlander, D-N.H., and Chrissy Houlahan, D-Pa., voted "present." Socialism has dominated the 2026 midterm election season on both sides of the aisle. Democrats are grappling with a far-left insurgency within their ranks as candidates linked to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) continue to topple incumbents and establishment-backed candidates across the country. It's provided fodder for the House GOP while it fights an uphill battle to keep control of Congress in November as Republicans warn the socialist left will take over the Democratic Party if it wins. "Socialism has failed everywhere it's been tried without exception. It's a dangerous ideology that creates misery for the very people it claims to help," Republican Study Committee Chairman August Pfluger, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital. "Today's vote puts the Left on the record and removes any doubt about where my colleagues on the other side of the aisle stand." Rep. Jeff Crank, R-Colo., who led the resolution, told Fox News Digital, "The resolution is pretty easy, right? It condemns socialism in all its forms, including the DSA, recommits ourselves to the Constitution of the United States…a third point is that we don't want non-citizens voting in elections." "They can certainly be critical, but it's just a quick choice for the American people to see where people stand on this stuff," Crank said. But Democrats contended that Republicans' largely symbolic resolution was a meaningless political exercise that does nothing to help Americans with their everyday problems. Many on the left have also dismissed the GOP's election integrity efforts as voter suppression. "So you're concerned about rising gas, or are you concerned about grocery prices? You know, don't worry. Republicans in Congress are passing another non-binding resolution condemning socialism," Rep. Jim McGovern, D-Mass., said during a hearing on Monday. The Tuesday evening vote would not have been possible without Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez rescuing Republicans' agenda. Golden is not running for re-election, while Gluesenkamp Perez is one of the most vulnerable Democrats in the country. It's almost unheard of for the minority party to help their political rivals pass a rule, and Jeffries told reporters he was not notified beforehand. The five House Republicans who voted against it were Reps. Pete Sessions, R-Texas; Chip Roy, R-Texas; Ralph Norman, R-S.C., Clay Higgins, R-La.; and Andy Harris, R-Md. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The rebels' issue was not with the measure itself, nor the bills it would have allowed the House to pass. Their votes were a protest against how their leaders handled a plan to avert a government shutdown just before the midterm elections, a short-term funding bill called a continuing resolution (CR). That measure passed just before the rule vote began. But the five GOP lawmakers took issue with how the Senate modified an original House-passed CR, including adding an unrelated measure to delay a congressionally approved hemp product ban by 30 days and a provision curbing the Trump administration’s control over federal grants. It's worth noting that Golden is also co-lead of a bill aimed at pausing new federal restrictions on certain American lobster and crab fishing industries, which would have also been stalled if the rule failed.

articles.title: Ted Cruz shuts down Trump Supreme Court talk with a fiery 'not just no, but hell no'
articles.summary: Sen. Ted Cruz told Sean Hannity his answer to a Supreme Court nomination from Trump would be "not just no, but hell no," despite his deep legal background.
articles.body: Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has dismissed speculation about a potential Supreme Court nomination, saying his response to President Donald Trump would be "not just no, but hell no." Speaking on the "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast, Cruz said he would rather remain in politics than serve on the Supreme Court. "So look, my answer is not just no, but hell no. And listen, I don't say that lightly. I mean, it’s a big deal. The court is an institution I revere," Cruz told Hannity. ALITO NOT EXPECTED TO RETIRE THIS TERM, COOLING SUPREME COURT VACANCY SPECULATION: SOURCES "And a lot of people are surprised, because I've spent an awful lot of my professional life around the court, in the court. And for so many people, it is their life dream to do," he added. Trump has floated Cruz’s name for the Supreme Court in the past, joking he’d be the only nominee to get "100% of the Democrat vote, 100% of the Republican vote" because lawmakers would want to "get him out" of Congress. TRUMP CHEERS ALITO STAYING FOR ANOTHER SUPREME COURT TERM: 'ONE OF THE GREATEST OF ALL TIME' Before entering politics, Cruz graduated from Princeton University and got his law degree from Harvard Law School. After law school, he clerked for Chief Justice William Rehnquist and later worked in private practice. During his conversation with Hannity, Cruz called Trump a "good friend," despite their rivalry during the 2016 Republican presidential primary. He also said that federal judges typically have to stay out of politics and policy battles. SUPREME COURT CHIEF JUSTICE PINPOINTS WHAT AMERICANS MISUNDERSTAND ABOUT HIM AND HIS COLLEAGUES "Because a principled federal judge stays out of politics and stays out of policy fights," Cruz said of why he would not want a seat on the bench. Cruz was sworn into the Senate in 2013. He previously served as solicitor general of Texas from 2003 to 2008 and argued nine cases before the U.S. Supreme Court. The Texas Tribune reported that Cruz was among 20 potential Supreme Court picks on Trump’s 2020 short list. Cruz responded to his inclusion on the list in a statement on X, then known as Twitter: "I am grateful for the president’s confidence in me and for his leadership in nominating principled constitutionalists to the federal bench over the last four years," Cruz said. "It’s humbling and an immense honor to be considered for the Supreme Court. The High Court plays a unique role in defending our Constitution, and there is no greater responsibility in public service than to support and defend the Constitution of the United States," he added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP At the time, Cruz said he had been "blessed to lead the fight to preserve our constitutional liberties" in the Senate and looked forward to continuing that work. Fox News's Alexandra Koch contributed to this report.

articles.title: The Alaska Senate race: 3 Republicans, 2 Dans Sullivan, 1 Democrat
articles.summary: Former Rep. Mary Peltola will be the only Democrat on the ballot after Democrat David Leslie, who finished fourth in the primary, withdrew.
articles.body: The Alaska Division of Elections on Tuesday named the four Senate candidates who will be on the ballot this fall in a closely watched race that will be decided by ranked-choice voting. Voters will make their selections among two Republicans named Dan Sullivan, another named Gerald Heikes and Democrat Mary Peltola, who finished first during the all-party primary in which the top four advance to the general election. Democrat David Leslie had finished fourth, but he withdrew from the race Monday. His withdrawal means fifth-place candidate Gerald Heikes, a Republican, will appear on the ballot. The race is considered one of the most competitive in the 2026 cycle and a potential pickup for Democrats, who are hoping to gain control of the Senate. It’s made headlines due to the novelty of having two candidates with the same first and last name. Dan J. Sullivan, a former schoolteacher who came in third in the primary, is seeking to unseat Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. But his candidacy has faced legal challenges from the senator and other Republicans who allege he is working with Peltola, a former congresswoman, and entered the race as a potential spoiler. He and Peltola have denied any coordination with each other, as have their campaigns. Although the Alaska Supreme Court allowed Sullivan to stay on the ballot after originally being disqualified by the Division of Elections, state and federal authorities are conducting their own investigation into his campaign. The Division of Elections on Tuesday also named general election candidates for the governor’s contest, including Republicans Dave Bronson and Bernadette Wilson and Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the top finisher in the primary. They are running to replace term-limited GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy. Tom Begich, a Democrat who finished second in the primary, withdrew from the race before Tuesday.

articles.title: Key Texas county votes to cut polling sites ahead of the midterms
articles.summary: Officials in Tarrant County, the third most-populous in Texas, approved a plan to reduce the number of polling locations by 92 compared to the 2022 elections.
articles.body: Officials in Texas’ third-largest county voted Tuesday to significantly reduce the number of polling sites for this fall’s midterm elections, drawing protests from Democrats and voting rights advocates. Commissioners in Tarrant County, a fast-growing and politically competitive area that includes Fort Worth, approved a plan that results in 92 fewer Election Day polling locations compared with the 2022 midterms. The roughly 30% reduction leaves the county with 224 polling sites to serve 1.3 million voters. Voters in the county are able to cast ballots at any of those polling sites. The three Republicans on the Tarrant County Commissioners Court voted for their plan, while the two Democrats voted against it. Research has found that each additional minute of travel time to a polling location can affect voter participation. The NAACP, the American Civil Liberties Union of Texas and other groups said in a letter that the changes would hit voters of color hardest because many of the reductions are in majority-minority areas in Fort Worth and Arlington. Supporters of the plan say that it will save money and that there are more than enough options for people to vote. The move comes amid a critical Senate contest in Texas, with Democratic state Rep. James Talarico taking on state Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican. Talarico urged the county to reject the plan ahead of Tuesday’s vote. “The most powerful people in this county, the most powerful people in this country, don’t want us to be able to vote easily,” Talarico told reporters Sunday, according to The Associated Press. Tarrant County has emerged as a key political battleground in Texas. President Donald Trump won it in the 2024 presidential race after Joe Biden flipped it four years prior. And Democrats Beto O’Rourke and Colin Allred narrowly carried the county in the 2018 and 2024 Senate races, respectively, even as they both went on to lose. Texas law gives counties the power to decide how many polling sites they use. And some counties have begun using fewer sites as they have moved to countywide voting in recent years. Dozens of voters urged the commissioners to vote against the cuts. Some criticized the elimination of specific polling places — like one at the University of Texas at Arlington — while others noted that the county has experienced significant population growth and voter participation in recent years. “The right to vote is the bedrock of our democracy,” said a woman named Linda Northern. “This will make it harder for brown, Black and low-income voters to have the same right to vote as you do. This is wrong.” Tarrant County Commissioner Roderick Miles Jr., a Democrat, added ahead of the vote, “This is about ensuring that the rights that people bled and died for are accessible to everybody.” Tarrant County Judge Tim O’Hare, a Republican on the commissioner court, argued that Miles wanted more polling sites in his area. “There’s no argument to that that you can come up with other than you want to be able to have more in your precinct,” O’Hare said. A handful of speakers supported the plan, noting that some sites were used by few voters and required a significant number of poll workers and financial resources. “I support the proposition that’s in front of us as far as reducing the number of voting sites. I’ve been a poll watcher, a poll worker, a precinct chair and all those things, and when you vote, when you go to a poll place that had 34 people all day long, you think this is kind of a waste of resources,” said one speaker, who did not identify herself.

articles.title: Former Florida governor hopeful hauled out of county meeting after protesting Israel investments
articles.summary: James Fischback was forcibly removed from a Miami-Dade commissioners meeting after protesting the county's raised investment limit in Israel bonds.
articles.body: James Fischback, a former Florida gubernatorial candidate and controversial political figure, was forcibly removed from a Miami-Dade Board of County Commissioners meeting Tuesday afternoon after protesting the county's expanded investment in Israel-backed bonds. "Do you serve the people of Hialeah or of Haifa? Do you serve the people of Aventura or of Tel Aviv? Do you serve the people of South Miami or of Jerusalem? This money should be invested here in this community. It should be invested in Miami-Dade County," he added before officers escorted him from the room. The confrontation comes after the county voted earlier this summer to raise its investment cap with Israel from 3% to 5% of its portfolio — a move that allows it invest upwards of about $400 million to $450 million. The change has drawn opposition from figures like Fischback critical of using public funds to invest in Israel as the war in Gaza continues to fuel political divisions in the U.S. It has also provided Fischback a platform to continue his opposition to U.S.-Israel ties. ANTISEMITISM FIGHT EXPLODES IN FLORIDA AS VOTERS HEAD TO THE POLLS: 'POLITICAL POGROM' "What this is about, very simply, is whom do you serve?" Fischback said. Fischback, a Republican, has garnered national attention for his views on race and has developed a reputation for confrontational public appearances. Fischback was among the 11 GOP candidates seeking to replace outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis. He garnered 10.4% of the vote in the Aug. 18 primary but drew national attention for a series of inflammatory on-camera moments. In one such case, he repeatedly called Rep. Byron Donalds, the frontrunner, eventual nominee and one of the only Black Republicans in Congress, a "slave" repeatedly at a news conference. "Byron Donalds is a slave. I’m sorry, he’s a slave. He is a slave to his donors. He is a slave to the corporate interests, to the tech bros that want to turn our state into, in his own words, a financial capital," Fischback said. He would later shout a similar phrase at Donalds directly, catching Donalds on the way back to his car with a megaphone and a throng of supporters. "You’re a DEI hire. You’re a slave. Go back to New York," Fischback yelled. JOSH SHAPIRO WARNS THAT ATTACKS ON AIPAC ARE BEING USED TO 'SILENCE CERTAIN VOTERS' Fischback's comments on Tuesday weren't the only ones that expressed outrage over the portfolio change. Other members of the public who expressed concern about the change voiced disappointment that the county would put public investment dollars behind Israel, given the politically charged atmosphere around the topic of its relations with the U.S. Another woman who identified herself as Ivar Fandel walked to the podium wearing a "let Gaza live" shirt. "Item 5B does exist in the context of a budget crisis as well as a genocide against Palestinians in Gaza at the hands of Israel," Fandel said, referring to the agenda item discussing the county's change. During his campaign, Fischback positioned himself as one of the only Republican candidates to decline contributions from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC). He also pledged to divest from Israel-backed bonds. "Florida has a specific policy. You’re not allowed to use taxpayer funds to buy foreign government bonds, with one exception: Israel. And so my premise is, first principles, we should not be lending taxpayer pensioner money to any foreign government," Fischback said in an interview with the American Conservative. He also blasted several candidates, including Donalds, for what he characterized as "singular allegiance" to Israel. HUCKABEE WARNS OF 'BIBLICAL IGNORANCE' AS HE DEFENDS CONSERVATIVE SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "I think people like Randy Fine and other AIPAC politicians have a singular allegiance. And that allegiance is to the best interests of Israel. The idea of saying ‘I am running to represent a foreign country’s interest in the United States Congress’ is preposterous. They’re buying allegiance," Fischback said in a post to X. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fischback did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Putin: German measures over Leipzig drone attack 'serious mistake'
articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin has called German punitive measures against Russia over a failed attack involving an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig airpor...
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has called German punitive measures against Russia over a failed attack involving an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig airport a "serious mistake" and rejected Berlin's accusations against Moscow.

"Where is the evidence?" Putin asked at a press conference in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek. He dismissed evidence presented so far as "fabricated" and said the response by Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government was primarily driven by domestic politics.

"Merz has lost the trust of citizens because he is not protecting Germany's national interests," Putin said following a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO). He said the future of Germany's current political leadership would be at stake in upcoming elections due to the country's economic problems.

Germany on Tuesday said Russia was responsible for the failed attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said police investigations, patterns of criminal activity and intelligence findings pointed to Russian responsibility for the attempted attack.

A drone fitted with explosives and a detonation mechanism was discovered on August 4 in the security zone of the airport, between Ukrainian cargo aircraft, prompting a temporary halt to flights.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul announced measures in response, including the closure of the Russian consulate general in Bonn on September 18 and the termination of the lease for the Russian House, a Russian cultural institution in the heart of Berlin.

articles.title: DOJ lawsuit targets alleged school ‘secret gender transitions’ policies that keep parents in the dark
articles.summary: The DOJ lawsuit against Kansas City, Kansas Public Schools alleges 'secret' gender transition plans locked parents out, violating FERPA and PPRA.
articles.body: The Department of Justice (DOJ) is investigating other school districts and contemplating additional lawsuits over alleged violations of federal parental rights laws, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon told Fox News Digital on Tuesday, calling the DOJ's newly filed "first-of-its-kind" case against Kansas City, Kansas Public Schools the "first of many." The DOJ sued Kansas City, Kansas Public Schools, aka KCKPS, on Tuesday, alleging the district violated the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA), and the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment (PPRA) with a district policy that facilitates "secret gender transitions" for students at school without their parents’ knowledge or consent. "No, we're not waiting. What we do is we ask for documents, we investigate, and then we try to resolve cases with school districts. And if we cannot, then we file lawsuits. And so there are many other lawsuits contemplated here and other investigations that are ongoing," Dhillon said when asked whether DOJ would wait for the Kansas case to conclude before pursuing other districts. Dhillon declined to identify the other districts under investigation, saying she did not want to prejudge the outcomes. EXCLUSIVE: HOUSE COMMITTEE PROBES CHICAGO PUBLIC SCHOOLS OVER HIDING 'GENDER AFFIRMATION' FROM PARENTS "This is a really important lawsuit for us. And the point I wanted to emphasize is that it's the first of many," she said. The DOJ lawsuit against KCKPS centers on internal guidance for transgender and gender non-conforming students. DOJ alleges the district has used versions of the guidance since 2017. Under the guidance described in the complaint, students can ask that their parents be excluded from school planning meetings and that their transgender or gender non-conforming status not be disclosed to them. The resulting written plans can address names, pronouns, school records, restroom and locker room use, sports and other accommodations. Asked about KCKPS’ assertion that it complies with federal law, Dhillon rejected the district’s position. FIRST ON FOX: SCHOOL LIED, HID DAUGHTER'S GENDER TRANSITION UNDER DISTRICT POLICY, PARENTS ALLEGE "Well, I think you can get that from the complaint, but they had secret gender transition plans that locked parents out of knowing what was being asked of their children. So I obviously completely reject that," Dhillon said. KCKPS disputed DOJ’s allegations Tuesday in a news release. "Contrary to the allegations in the Complaint, the district maintains that it is in full compliance with FERPA and PPRA and is disappointed by the DOJ’s decision to file the lawsuit," the release read. The district said it would respond through the federal court process and would not comment further while the litigation is pending. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION THREATENS KANAS SCHOOL DISTRICT FUNDING OVER TRANSGEDNER STUDENT POLICY The DOJ argues the written plans constitute education records under FERPA, and that excluding parents can prevent them from exercising their rights to inspect and challenge those records. The government separately alleges the district violates PPRA by allowing students to participate in meetings and evaluations that can reveal sensitive information without prior written parental consent. The Department of Education opened a FERPA investigation into KCKPS in August 2025. The federal government advised the district on Aug. 12 that its guidance violated FERPA and PPRA, and the complaint states the government ultimately determined KCKPS would not voluntarily comply. DOJ is asking a federal court to declare the district’s practices unlawful and prohibit enforcement of the guidance or similar policies that violate FERPA or PPRA. Dhillon said DOJ intends to pursue potential violations elsewhere. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "But I want there to be a very clear message to every. School district in the United States. They are on notice that if they violate FERPA and PPRA, the United State's Department of Justice stands ready to protect the rights of parents and the rights to pupils to privacy, dignity, and parental rights in determining how children are educated in the united states," Dhillon said. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Kansas referred questions about the lawsuit to the DOJ’s Office of Public Affairs.
